statements.anchor: The use of artificial intelligence or large language models is prohibited for all work in this course.
statements.label: AI prohibited for all work
statements.passage:
The use of artificial intelligence or large language models is prohibited for all work in this course.
You may not use these tools to summarize readings, generate discussion points, write reading journals, write code, or as any other type of resource.
This policy is designed to incentivize the activities that best support your learning: reading, thinking, discussing, and writing code on your own and with other students learning along with you.
If you are struggling with anything for this course you will get much more out of a conversation with the instructor, a mentor, or another student than you would from an AI tool generating a solution for you.

It is acceptable for you to use AI-generated summaries from search engines like Google as a starting point when you are looking for appropriate resources, but you must review and cite the actual sources of the information you use (usually linked at the end of the summary).
Citing the AI tool is not appropriate, as it is synthesizing information from other sources.
These summaries have improved, but they are still prone to misrepresenting the information in the actual sources they cite.
It is your responsibility to accurately cite the source of information and ideas you use, so review the source carefully.

You should be aware that AI tools often produce similar code for different users, so if you chose to violate course policy and use an AI tool to complete a programming assignment, you could easily end up submitting work that is nearly identical to another student’s work.
If I see these kinds of similarities in students’ work I am obligated to report them as an academic honesty violation, even if I do not know whether the similarity is the result of inappropriate collaboration or inappropriate AI use.

Academic integrity and collaboration

statements.passage:
You are always responsible for the full authorship and accountability for your work. Misrepresenting the output of other people as your own original work is a serious breach of academic integrity standards.

Where does AI fit?
As noted above, LLMs are an industry-expected toolset for helping create software source-code. That said, there are students who do not want to use AI or who constrain their AI use in a variety of ways. It is possible to thrive in CS5 without AI at all (many generations of students have done so!), and you are welcome not to use it. You are also welcome to use it under constraints of your choosing -- chat with the instructor(s) if you have concerns about this.
(Within the
HMC AI-use guidelines
, cs5's AI-use score is student-chosen, between perhaps a
0.42
and
4.2
. That is, prompt-space is
never required
, even if LLMs are, naturally,
part of the curriculum
itself
. AI is just a computational process, after all. Its use is also invited-and-welcome, because experience is an nontrivial educator -- and a nontrivial share of software's professional landscape does expect it.)

It's also true that a growing subset of professional paths expect sophistication with computing and AI
together
. For example, applied computer science -- even far from software-engineering or software-centric roles -- seeks

source-code and software
control

(the ability, just-in-time, to change artifacts in order to match your and others' newly intended behaviors)
and

source-code and software
communication

(the ability to convey the underlying mechanisms-of-operation to others, and to yourself)
--

source-code and software
accountability

(vouching for and demonstrating the ability to handle expected and unexpected behavior in one's software systems)
--

These three skills are
more
valuable than ever,
because they no longer always get the "free-ride" that comes when source is
personally
generated!

To serve as wide an audience as possible
, cs5 encourages the development of these professionally and personally valuable skills (including the use of AI -- for those interested in honing their skills with it).

statements.label: AI allowed for tools and background
statements.passage:
Other sources, most commonly web searches and LLM queries, are treated similarly to collaboration with other (non-partner) people: you can use these resources to help you use tools and technology, or for getting alternate or additional instruction/background on lecture topics, but they may not be used in place of developing a solution to an assigned problem.
If you find a particularly helpful resource to augment what I provide, share it with the whole class!
LLMs are especially tricky because they probably can provide solutions to many of the assigned problems and, unlike a classmate, do not account for the expectations of the class or the integrity of your learning process. You are responsible for being cautious with your queries to avoid accidentally generating a solution. As with any other source, if you inadvertently gain access to a solution, you are responsible for self-reporting rather than taking credit for work that you did not produce.
We will use Google Colab for programming assignments which, these days, automatically includes LLM-generated code suggestions. You
may
make use of this feature if you wish (unless otherwise specified), but remember that you are coding to deepen your understanding, not simply to get the assignment done. Even when Colab makes suggestions, you should be clear in your intent for the code you are writing so you can evaluate its suggestions. You should of course always seek to understand the code that you submit; this is perhaps even more true when some of the code is recommended by an LLM.

statements.label: AI treated like helpful friend
statements.passage:
In all respects, using AI (such as ChatGPT or GitHub Copilot) is equivalent to turning to a friend who has already taken the class and asking them for help—the same rules apply. It would not be okay to have a friend do your homework for you, or sit next to you telling you at each moment what to write next.

The AI usage rules below are thus just a restatement of the general principles above, with a focus on how they apply to AI tools.

Your Responsibilities

Unlike other sources of help who may naturally exercise their own good judgment in deciding what information to provide, you may need to take explicit steps to prevent AI tools and assistants from inadvertently providing you with answers or solutions that you should be developing on your own. For example, Visual Studio Code makes it very easy to turn on GitHub Copilot and receive suggestions for code completions, causing AI to write code that was supposed to be your own work. It is your responsibility to ensure that you can tell whether AI code completions are enabled or not and ensure that they are
disabled
while working on code for this class.

Likewise, if you ask an AI assistant such as ChatGPT a question about assignment materials or code, there is a good chance that the assistant will be too direct in giving you solutions, giving you an unfair advantage over your classmates, undermining your own learning process, and potentially violating the Honor Code. One way to avoid such issues is to avoid using AI assistants for direct help with assignments or code (conceptual discussions about lesson materials would be okay). Talking to a grutor or your professor, or posting your about your issue on Piazza, will avoid these kinds of challenges.

appropriately, they may assist in brainstorming, exploring
ideas, and refining drafts. However,
they must never
replace your own intellectual work
.

programming tutors, and lab assistants: they can guide and support
but must not generate final submissions.

content primarily generated by AI is a violation of academic
integrity
, comparable to submitting work completed
by someone else.

your
original understanding, reasoning, and
expression
.

and revised, and any challenges or limitations encountered.

statements.passage:
Generative AI and Your Learning

Academic honesty
includes the appropriate use of technology as an aid for learning and productivity. This includes but is not limited to LLM-based generative artificial intelligence tools such as Claude, GPT, Gemini, Mistral, Perplexity, DeepSeek, Kimi, Copilot, Meta AI, Grok, and NotebookLM.

Modern GenAI provides fast solutions to a variety of computing problems but must be used responsibly to get the most out of your education. In some cases it may struggle to write code for scenarios it cannot recognize, producing bugs and security vulnerabilities, making things worse for you. It will not be available for job interviews. You have a moral and ethical responsibility to deeply understand every line of software you produce, whether by hand or by directing an agent, and should therefore employ GenAI only when its use does not rob you of the stretch-zone learning that comes from crafting programs on your own.

As a learner developing skills in reading and writing code, limit the use of GenAI in programmatic assignments to the following cases:

Generating short documentation strings and type hints.

Finding examples and explanations for syntactic forms (e.g., How do I use the spread operator? How do I construct a dictionary comprehension? How do I unwrap an optional? and so on). Prompt the AI for the how-to’s,
not
your final code.

Interpreting error messages, as these might be pretty cryptic! Often the AI will be a fantastic tutor when explaining things it
is
familiar with.

Generating unit tests for edge cases. When it finds something you overlooked, make a mental or written note so you can find these cases on your own next time.

Scanning the code you
have
written yourself for errors, inefficiencies, vulnerabilities, or potential improvements.

Remember the four As
DO use technologies such as GenAI to
augment ✅
,
amplify ✅
, and
accelerate ✅
your learning; NEVER use technology to
avoid ❌
learning.
Treat GenAI as an assistant, not a subcontractor.

Be responsible!
Using GenAI and related tools without knowing what you are doing may lead to poor homework submissions that rarely achieve a grade higher than an F on their own merits, simply due to hallucinations and an inability to carry out tasks exactly as they were assigned (even with good prompts).
Instructors and TAs are GenAI users themselves and will be able to easily detect inappropriate student use of these tools. The teaching staff will try to steer you back on track s

Generative AI and Your Learning

Academic honesty
includes the appropriate use of technology as an aid for learning and productivity. This includes but is not limited to LLM-based generative artificial intelligence tools such as Claude, GPT, Gemini, Mistral, Perplexity, DeepSeek, Kimi, Copilot, Meta AI, Grok, and NotebookLM.

Modern GenAI provides fast solutions to a variety of computing problems but must be used responsibly to get the most out of your education. In some cases it may struggle to write code for scenarios it cannot recognize, producing bugs and security vulnerabilities, making things worse for you. It will not be available for job interviews. You have a moral and ethical responsibility to deeply understand every line of software you produce, whether by hand or by directing an agent, and should therefore employ GenAI only when its use does not rob you of the stretch-zone learning that comes from crafting programs on your own.
